style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Now I'll show you three templates we recommend for the closing paragraph.
One: the benefits summary. This is the default. The one to use.
Two: the essay summary. That's for more advanced writers.
And three... my favourite. The time-pressure line.
Okay, the benefits summary. First, my position. That's the answer to the question we're discussing.
Then the first benefit or harm, from argument paragraph one. Then the second one, from argument paragraph two.
It's as simple as that.
Let's see where each part comes from.
Your position is the last sentence of the opening. Go there, and take it. That's the start of your closing.
Then go to the key sentence of argument one. Remember what it looks like: I'm for or against something, because it will bring this benefit, or that harm.
Take its second half, the benefit, and put it here.
Same thing with paragraph two. Copy the second half of its key sentence. The benefit, or the harm. That's all.
Here are some phrase options, so it's not always the same sentence.
The idea is to use the right connectors. Cause and effect, and then addition.
Here's an example for the cameras.
I answered the question we're discussing. That's exactly the last line of my opening.
Benefit one: deterrence, which reduces harm to citizens. I took it from argument paragraph one. The second half of its key sentence.
Benefit two: saving resources.
A short, excellent closing. Nothing to complain about, zero mistakes. Like they say... less is more. And this is the place for it.
The second template sums up the whole essay. And that's really what a closing is for. But it fits more advanced structures.
What I recommend is, don't start with it. Start with the benefits summary. Move to this one only when you feel you're getting better, and you want to push higher.
Remember the rebuttal paragraph? The opposing argument, its explanation, and then the weakening. So I take the weakening from there.
It's a full, rich paragraph that really sums up the essay. But notice... it's not in the essay's order.
In the essay it was argument one, argument two, then the counterargument, and then the weakening. So why change the order?
Well, first, it just fits together better. You'll see that in the example.

And second, people remember the end best. I want to leave the rater with my position. So I open with the counterargument, give my view, weaken it, add benefit one and benefit two... and that's the feeling they're left with.
Here's an example, for the cameras.
The counterargument: a risk to privacy. My position: even so, install the cameras.
Why? That's the weakening. Safeguards can keep the harm to a minimum.
Moreover... I didn't only weaken the counterargument. I have more advantages. Deterrence, and saving resources.
Now, it's not like we're always for the cameras. Here's the other side.
The counterargument: crime in the monitored areas would go down.
Here I didn't write 'but in my view, cameras should not be installed'. I used an expression: a zero-sum game.

So what's a zero-sum game? One side pulls this way, the other side pulls that way, and we end up at zero. Plus five, minus five. The offender stops stealing in the monitored area, so he steals somewhere else, just as often as before.
That's my weakening, explained. Then harm one: serious harm to privacy. And harm two: the danger that the database leaks, and the information is used to hurt people.
And now, a template I think is really cool. The time-pressure line.

A lot of the time, you get to the end of the essay with no time left. You got stuck somewhere. Planning and writing an essay in thirty-five minutes isn't easy. Many students barely finish the closing.
So you state your position, and you say its advantages outweigh its disadvantages. Fixed wording. One sentence.
For example: in conclusion, face-recognition cameras should be installed in public spaces, since, as shown above, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. That's it.
If your essay up to the closing is excellent, then with this line and a half, it stays excellent. The closing doesn't add points. The score was set before the rater got there.
We've seen quite a few essays that end with no closing at all.
So know this. Even an excellent essay without a closing loses points.
If you're short on time, don't give up, don't panic, and don't write half a paragraph. Like, a position, then a benefit, and then stopping in the middle of the sentence. No.
Not under time pressure? Use the benefits summary. Or the essay summary, if you want something more advanced. Under time pressure? The one-line template.
